````markdown
- Show changes: <off | summary | full>
- Default mode: <mode name>
- Glossary pack: <design | product | engineering | marketing | general | none>

<!-- App-specific settings (model tier, drafts folder) live in config.md, not here, so this file travels cleanly between apps. -->

## Core voice

### Who I am

<One or two lines: what they do, who they usually write for, anything that shapes how they sound. Only what they said.>

### The register in one line

<For example: "First person, warm, plain, a little dry.">

### Voice

| Dimension | My choice | Example I picked or wrote |
|---|---|---|
| Funny or serious | | |
| Formal or casual | | |
| Respectful or irreverent | | |
| Enthusiastic or matter-of-fact | | |
| Opening | | |
| Stating a point or decision | | |
| Technical level | | |
| Results and numbers | | |
| Limits and bad news | | |
| Contractions | | |
| Sentence length and rhythm | | |
| Personality | | |

### How I talk

<Speech patterns from the interview and transcripts: where the point usually lands, favourite fillers, how they correct themselves, how they explain things to a friend, words dictation often mishears.>

### Stories and phrases I reuse

<Stories they retell, metaphors and turns of phrase that are recognisably theirs, in their words. Use these only when they fit what the person is actually saying; never insert one to add personality.>

### My rules

- Dashes (— –): <use freely | sparingly | never>
- Words I never want: <list>
- Words I like: <list>
- Emoji and exclamation marks: <never | only in some modes | fine>
- Patterns I'm fine with: <catalogue patterns to leave alone, by name or ID, e.g. "lists of three when there really are three">
- Other: <e.g. "say 'people' not 'users'", "sign off with just my first name">

### My terms

<Plain description → the term they want. These win over any glossary pack. A term never changes status, scale or evidence: a prototype stays a prototype, "a few people" stays vague, "tried it" never becomes "validated". Such a row is refused, with the reason.>

| When I say | Write |
|---|---|

### Fingerprint

<Measured from their own unassisted writing by `scripts/voice_stats.py` (see `editing/fingerprint.md`). A plain-English table, then the full numbers. If no script was available, write "Not measured yet" and leave out the marker and the JSON block.>

### Learned

<Corrections they asked to remember for every mode, newest at the bottom, each dated. These override the style choices above. They can never switch off the truth rules: a learned entry never adds, upgrades or hides a claim. Mark replaced entries "(replaced <date>)".>

## Modes

<One subsection per place they write. A mode holds only what's different from the core voice. Built-in shapes live in `modes/`; a custom mode describes its own shape here. Add or remove modes with the Voices job.>

### Mode: <name, e.g. LinkedIn>

- Shape: <built-in mode file name, e.g. social-post, or "custom: see below">
- Reader: <who reads this and what they want from it>
- Adjustments to my core voice: <e.g. "shorter paragraphs, one idea per line, no hashtags, end on a question only if I really want an answer">

#### Examples

<Passages from their own writing for this mode, quoted exactly, grouped by the job each one does (openings, explaining a point, decisions, results, closings, sign-offs...). 2 to 8 per job is plenty. Leave out jobs their samples don't cover.>

#### Learned in this mode

<Corrections that apply only here, dated. These win over the core Learned section for this mode.>

<!-- end of voice file -->
````

## File: `references/glossaries/_how-to-use.md`

# How to use the term lists

Each list maps how people *describe* something when talking to the term a senior person in that field would *write*. Use a term only when it means exactly what the person described. If two terms could fit, ask. Never swap in a term that implies a more formal method, a bigger sample or a measured result than the person described. Prefer the plainer term when both are accurate: precise is better than jargon-heavy. The person's own *My terms* in the voice file always win over these lists.

Contributions welcome: add rows to a list, or add a new list for another field.


## File: `references/glossaries/design.md`

# Design terms

| When they say something like | Term |
|---|---|
| a huge board you can pan around, click and drag on | interactive canvas (infinite canvas if it has no edges) |
| the frame or page you design on | artboard / frame |
| boxes that each hold a bit of content | cards |
| the bar at the bottom with the main tabs | bottom navigation / tab bar |
| the menu that slides in from the side | navigation drawer / side sheet |
| the panel that slides up from the bottom | bottom sheet |
| the popup in the middle you have to deal with | modal / dialog |
| the round floating button | floating action button |
| small rounded tags you tap to filter | filter chips |
| the row you scroll sideways | horizontal carousel |
| the line that shows which step you're on | progress indicator / stepper |
| splitting a long form into pages | multi-step form |
| putting related things together | grouping / chunking |
| making the most important thing look most important | visual hierarchy |
| how everything is organised and named | information architecture |
| the same layout working on phone and desktop | responsive layout |
| hiding the advanced stuff until it's needed | progressive disclosure |
| sections that open and close | accordion |
| the screen before there's any content | empty state |
| the screen saying it worked | success state / confirmation screen |
| grey placeholder boxes while it loads | skeleton screen / loading state |
| it checks your answer as you type | inline validation |
| it remembers where you were | saved progress / auto-save |
| a little hint next to the field | helper text |
| the right keyboard pops up for each field | input types / contextual keyboards |
| bigger buttons so you don't miss them | larger touch targets |
| people tapping again and again in frustration | rage taps / rage clicks |
| the small animation when you tap | micro-interaction |
| the message that pops up and disappears | toast / snackbar |
| the main button | primary action |
| already filled in with a sensible answer | sensible default |
| a quick clickable version | prototype |
| rough boxes and lines | wireframes |
| the shared buttons, colours and rules | design system / component library |
| named colour and spacing values | design tokens |
| the flowchart of screens and choices | user flow / task flow |
| the map of everything someone goes through | journey map |
| watched recordings of people using it | session recordings |
| sat with people and watched them try it | usability sessions (moderated sessions only if they ran them as such; ask) |
| looked at what other apps do | competitor review |
| where people gave up | drop-off |
| usable by everyone, including with a screen reader | accessible / accessibility |


## File: `references/glossaries/engineering.md`

# Engineering terms

| When they say something like | Term |
|---|---|
| the part people see | front end / client |
| the part on the server | back end |
| how the app talks to the server | API |
| where the data is kept | database / data store |
| it keeps working without internet | offline support |
| it syncs between devices | sync |
| keeping a copy so it loads faster | caching |
| it got slow when lots of people used it | didn't scale / performance under load |
| it fell over | outage / incident |
| we put it out | shipped / deployed / released |
| we can undo the release | rollback |
| tests that run automatically | automated tests / CI |
| the old code nobody wants to touch | legacy code / tech debt |
| we rebuilt it without changing what it does | refactor |
| two things fighting over the same data | race condition |
| only some people can see it | access control / permissions |
| logging in | authentication |
| what you're allowed to do once logged in | authorisation |
| a program that runs on a schedule | scheduled job / cron job |
| plugging into another company's service | integration / third-party API |


## File: `references/glossaries/general.md`

# General terms (for any field)

| When they say something like | Write |
|---|---|
| it was all over the place | inconsistent |
| people just gave up | people abandoned it / dropped off |
| I sort of led it | I led it (if they did), or I contributed to it (if they didn't): ask |
| we kind of tested it | we tested it with <n> people: ask how many |
| it worked way better | it improved <what> from <x> to <y>: ask for the numbers |
| a bunch of | several / <the actual number, if they gave one; otherwise keep it vague or ask> |
| stuff | <the actual things> |
| super important | important |
| basically | (cut) |
| at the end of the day | (cut) |

# Marketing and communication terms

| When they say something like | Term |
|---|---|
| who we're talking to | audience / target segment |
| what makes us different | positioning / differentiator |

## File: `references/glossaries/product.md`

# Product terms

| When they say something like | Term |
|---|---|
| the steps and how many people get through each | funnel |
| where people gave up | drop-off / abandonment |
| people came back | retention |
| people stopped using it | churn |
| the first time someone uses it | onboarding / first-run experience |
| the moment they get why it's useful | activation / moment of value |
| the one number we cared about most | the main metric (north-star metric only if they call it that) |
| we tried two versions to see which did better | ask: a live split test on real traffic (A/B test), or two versions shown to a few people (compared two versions)? |
| we released it to some people first | staged rollout / beta |
| switched it on for some users only | feature flag |
| the smallest version we could ship | MVP / first release |
| what people are really trying to get done | the job to be done / user goal |
| deciding what to build first | prioritisation |
| the plan for the next few months | roadmap |
| things we chose not to do | out of scope / trade-offs |
| problems we already know about | known issues |
| what it costs us vs what we get | cost versus benefit (ROI only if they measured it) |
| the people who have a say | stakeholders |
| rules we had to follow | regulatory constraints / compliance |
| how we'll know it worked | success criteria |

## File: `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`

# Third-party notices

Natural Voice is MIT licensed: see the LICENSE file that comes with it, or [LICENSE on GitHub](https://github.com/nishjaiswal/natural-voice/blob/main/LICENSE). Its editing guidance draws on the work below. This file says what we used, how we used it, and under what terms. It lives in the skill folder so it ships with every copy of the skill.

Last checked: 8 October 2026.

## Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing

- **What it is:** a field guide to patterns in AI-generated text, written and maintained by volunteers in WikiProject AI Cleanup. [Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing). We read [the revision of 8 October 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing&oldid=1379229123).
- **How we used it:** as a source of patterns, dates and model differences for `references/editing/pattern-catalogue.md`. We describe every pattern in our own words and wrote our own examples. No sentences were copied. Where we repeat single words from its lists (for example the model word lists by era), we credit it next to them.
- **Licence:** Wikipedia text is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 licence (CC BY-SA 4.0). We copied no text, so our files are not under that licence. If you add text from that page to this project, you must follow CC BY-SA 4.0 for that text.

## Humanizer

- **What it is:** an MIT-licensed agent skill by Siqi Chen that rewrites AI-sounding text. [blader/humanizer](https://github.com/blader/humanizer). We compared against version 3.1.0.
- **How we used it:** its grouping of patterns, its idea that some patterns count only in clusters ("weak alone"), some of its group names (for example "Inflation and borrowed authority", "Formatting by rule" and "Writing for the wrong reader"), and about ten of its pattern headings, reused word for word (for example "One-line closers and dramatic fragments", "Arguing with no one" and "Re-explaining what the reader knows"). The catalogue cites Humanizer's pattern numbers (§1 to §26) so readers can compare. Our descriptions, examples and rules are our own. We also cite [Humanizer issue #229](https://github.com/blader/humanizer/issues/229) (19 August 2026), an informal study of rewrite quality and detection.

## Graphite research

- [AI Tells](https://graphite.io/five-percent/research/ai-tells) (16 September 2026) and [AI Tells: Opus 5.5 update](https://graphite.io/five-percent/research/ai-tells-opus-5-5-update) (1 October 2026), by Gregory Druck, Jose Luis Paredes and Ethan Smith at Graphite.
- We quote their phrase ratios as facts, with credit. Their figures come from one corpus of web articles and one fixed prompt. Graphite is a marketing firm and the work is not peer reviewed, so the catalogue marks these figures as secondary.
- Coverage we also read: [TechCrunch, 1 October 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/01/opus-5-5-loves-to-tell-you-this-matters-and-other-ai-writing-tells/).

We state facts from these pages with links, and quote short phrases only. The Economist's article "How to spot AI writing" (30 July 2026) is cited as secondary, because we read it only through other reports.

- Anthropic: [How Claude's text watermark works](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-text-watermark) and [How Claude marks AI-generated content](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/16266773-how-claude-marks-ai-generated-content)

- C2PA: [Content Credentials specification 2.4](https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.4/specs/C2PA_Specification.html)

- Epoch AI: [AI detectors and false negatives](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/ai-detectors-false-negatives)
- Detector vendors' help pages: Turnitin, Grammarly, GPTZero and Pangram, linked from `references/editing/detectors-and-watermarks.md`
